title: Holiness Theme
summary: Leviticus calls Israel to be holy because God is holy, then gives that call practical shape in the chapter’s commands about worship, justice, honesty, and care for neighbors. Isaiah’s vision of God’s holiness makes the prophet aware of his own unclean speech, which is purified before he is sent. First Peter quotes Leviticus as it calls its readers to holy conduct, and Hebrews urges peace and holiness. Across these passages, holiness joins worship, character, and communal life rather than naming only ritual separation.
historical_context: The passages present holiness in distinct settings. Leviticus 19 places the call to holiness at the start of a chapter of commands for Israel’s life together. Isaiah 6 portrays the prophet’s vision of the holy LORD, his confession of unclean lips, and his cleansing before service. First Peter 1:13–16 applies Leviticus’ call to the conduct of its readers, while Hebrews 12:14 urges them to pursue peace and holiness. The later passages reuse the Leviticus command in their own exhortations.
literary_context: Leviticus 19 opens with a direct command and grounds it in God’s holiness; the rest of the chapter shows how that calling shapes concrete obligations toward God and neighbor. Isaiah 6 uses a throne-room vision, where the repeated cry “Holy, holy, holy” leads to the prophet’s confession, cleansing, and commission. First Peter quotes Leviticus within an exhortation to live differently, and Hebrews 12:14 places holiness beside the pursuit of peace. The different forms show how the theme moves from command and vision to communal instruction.
covenantal_significance: Holiness marks life belonging to God and changes how people treat one another. Leviticus ties the call to holiness to communal obligations; Isaiah’s cleansing prepares a prophet for service; and the New Testament passages connect holiness with conduct and peace. The theme should not be reduced to a label of contamination or used to excuse coercion or harm. The linked CKL evidence treats communal holiness as involving belonging, non-harm, accountability, and restoration.
canonical_role: Holiness Theme serves as a thematic anchor, connecting repeated biblical patterns, key passages, and related theological concepts across the canon.

related_objects.notes: The cluster joins body ethics to belonging, non-harm, consent, accountability, transformation, and restoration rather than contamination status.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Holiness Theme in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
